newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil sees better trade balance, for a few months.
newsitem.headline: Brazil sees better trade balance, for a few months.

text.p: The Brazilian government expects the trade outlook to improve over the next few months but realizes that the second half of 1997 could again see widening trade deficits, officials said Tuesday.

Mauricio Cortes, secretary of foreign trade at the Ministry of Industry and Commerce, said good prospects for the harvest, in particular for soybean, and favourable trends in international prices should boost exports as of April.
He added that International Monetary Fund forecasts of decent economic growth in main customers the European Union, Japan and the United States boded well for Brazilian agricultural exports.
"These countries buy 52 percent of our exports," Cortes said at a briefing to explain March's $1.027 billion trade gap, bringing the deficit for first quarter 1997 to $3.05 billion.

The foreign trade secretary also divulged a survey by various industrial sectors that indicated significant gains could be expected in overseas sales in 1997 because of exemption from the so-called ICMS export tax.

Among others, Coffee exports were expected to exceed 1996's by 57 percent or an extra $980 million in sales. Soybean shipments should rise 13 percent or $400 million and fresh fruit sales some 10.5 percent or $30 million.
Semi-manufactured goods were expected to be 20 percent higher, or an additional $117 million.
"Summed up, these mean an extra $1.82 billion, largely due to exemption from the ICMS tax," Cortes said.
But Jose Roberto Mendonca de Barros, economic policy secretary of the Finance Ministry, threw in a touch of caution.
Mendonca de Barros acknowledged that peak shipments from the harvest usually ran till June. "So something else will have to increase in the second half," he said.
Mendonca de Barros said recently imposed restrictions on short-term import financing would have an effect on the trade balance but declined to put that into figures.

He also noted that on a seasonally-adjusted basis, imports of $13.707 over the first three months of 1997, or of $4.853 billion in March, were "similar" to import levels over the second half of 1996, suggesting stability.
